analysis.one_liner: Let homeowners and renters pause mortgage payments, stop foreclosures and repossessions, and backstop lenders during the COVID emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Financial Services Committee with no vote and no further action after its introduction on March 23, 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any homeowner facing a pandemic hardship pause their mortgage payments for 180 days, extendable for another 180, by simply stating they were struggling — no paperwork required. It would have banned foreclosures, eviction actions after foreclosure, and repossessions of cars and manufactured homes during the emergency, required landlords receiving forbearance to pass relief to their tenants, and required lenders to offer affordable repayment plans afterward. To make that workable, it would have set up a Federal Reserve credit line for mortgage servicers and shielded compliant servicers from investor lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing pandemic income loss — including those whose loans were not federally backed and were left out of the relief that eventually passed — as well as tenants of landlords who received forbearance, and owners of financed cars and manufactured homes who would have been protected from repossession.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Struggling homeowners, renters, and car owners

how_it_helps.text: Any borrower experiencing COVID-19 hardship could request a 180-day forbearance (extendable 180 more) by affirming hardship, with no additional documentation, regardless of delinquency status [S3].

Servicers were barred from starting or continuing foreclosures and post-foreclosure evictions during the emergency and for 180 days after, except for vacant or abandoned homes, and barred from repossessing financed vehicles and manufactured homes in that same window [S3].

Landlords of five-plus-unit buildings who got forbearance could not evict tenants for nonpayment or charge them fees during the forbearance, and single-family borrowers receiving forbearance had to pass rent relief to their own tenants [S3].

After forbearance, servicers had to offer borrowers catch-up plans spread over time or loan modifications — including term extensions and principal reductions — with no late fees, penalty interest, or modification fees [S3].
Borrowers 60 or more days delinquent would be placed in forbearance automatically, and servicers had to notify borrowers of their rights on every statement, in English and other languages [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers and lenders, who would have advanced payments they never collected and absorbed deferred principal; mortgage investors in securitization trusts, who would have borne losses the bill's safe harbor insulates servicers from; and auto and manufactured-home lenders facing a repossession ban.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage servicers, investors, and vehicle lenders

drawbacks.text: Forbearance is a pause, not forgiveness: missed principal and interest still come due afterward, whether spread out, added to the loan balance, or handled through modification — households with lasting income loss still owed the money [S3].

Small landlords receiving forbearance on their buildings were required to give their own tenants rent relief, which could squeeze landlords whose main income was those rents while they still owed taxes and insurance [S3].

The bill would have created a Federal Reserve and Treasury credit line for mortgage servicers and a broad liability safe harbor, shifting the cost of the pause onto the Fed's balance sheet and mortgage investors rather than the industry that originated risky loans [S3].
A blanket ban on vehicle and manufactured-home repossessions without a compensating mechanism could have raised borrowing costs for the borrowers who keep paying [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core consumer protections — no-documentation forbearance, foreclosure and repossession freezes, tenant pass-through, and no-fee repayment plans — were strong and well targeted to a moment when millions abruptly lost income. The tradeoffs are real but mostly about who eats the cost of the pause: the bill deliberately pushed it onto servicers' balance sheets and then backstopped the servicers with a Fed credit facility and a lawsuit shield, a design that protects the industry's structure even as it regulates it. The servicer safe harbor is the provision an honest supporter would have to defend hardest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and nothing further ever happened to it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay introduced the bill on March 23, 2020 and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no further action — no markup, no floor vote, no committee report — was ever recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4][S5].

Four days after introduction, Congress enacted the CARES Act, which provided forbearance only for federally backed mortgages; this bill would have covered a broader set of loans and added foreclosure and repossession bans the CARES Act did not [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers, securitization investors, and vehicle lenders — they avoided a broader, no-documentation forbearance mandate and repossession ban, and the relief homeowners did get was the narrower CARES Act version limited to federally backed loans.

for.name: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee of referral — majority-controlled, took no action
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup, report, or floor scheduling for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split was recorded; the bill drew only one cosponsor, a fellow Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would have obligated servicers to grant forbearance and advance payments, but paired that duty with a Federal Reserve credit facility to fund the advances and a safe harbor from investor lawsuits, making servicers the permanent channel for pandemic mortgage relief at public backstopped cost. Servicer-friendly design was central to the bill's structure, not an afterthought.

Servicers could grant forbearance without breaching their duties to investors, and the bill's findings stated investors could not expect servicing contracts to be fully enforceable in a crisis — losses on the payment pause would land partly on them.
A blanket repossession ban for the emergency and 180 days after would have removed their main leverage over delinquent borrowers, raising their risk on those loans.

Landlords of five-plus-unit buildings could pause their mortgages, but in exchange could not evict tenants for nonpayment or charge fees during the forbearance and had to bring loans current within a year after it ended.
